item.title: ATP8B1–TMEM30B flippase activity maintains stereocilia lipid asymmetry required for hearing
item.author: Takesha Foster
item.content:encoded: Sensory hair cells convert sound-induced vibrations into electrical signals through a process called mechano-electrical transduction (MET). While the protein components of the MET complex are well studied, increasing evidence indicates that MET channel properties are significantly modulated by the surrounding lipid bilayer. The asymmetric distribution of membrane lipids between the inner and outer membrane leaflets is well established to shape membrane mechanics. The recent discovery that the core MET components TMC1 and TMC2 also act as lipid scramblases suggests a direct role for membrane lipid asymmetry in the dynamic shaping of auditory transduction. Because scramblase activity of TMC1/2 disrupts lipid asymmetry, we hypothesized that an opposing flippase may be required to restore and maintain lipid asymmetry. Here, we identify the P4-ATPase ATP8B1 and its chaperone TMEM30B as selectively expressed in mouse outer hair cells (OHCs), enriched in stereocilia, and upregulated following the onset of MET and hearing. Loss of either protein results in elevated auditory brainstem response (ABR) thresholds, phosphatidylserine (PS) externalization, and rapid hair-cell degeneration, demonstrating that lipid homeostasis is crucial for OHC survival. Together, these findings establish ATP8B1 and TMEM30B as key regulators of membrane lipid asymmetry in sensory hair cells and establish TMEM30B as a novel deafness gene.

item.title: Addressing Inconsistency in Functional Neuroimaging: A Replicable Data‐Driven Multi‐Scale Functional Atlas for Canonical Brain Networks
item.author: Kyle M. Jensen, Jessica A. Turner, Lucina Q. Uddin, Vince D. Calhoun, Armin Iraji
item.content:encoded: The NeuroMark multi-scale atlas is highly replicable across individuals, datasets, and studies and serves to establish a common reference space in neuroimaging research. Use of the atlas will help to standardize terminology and methodology in the field of neuroscience and reveal many insights into the brain.The advent of multiple neuroimaging methodologies has greatly aided in the conceptualization of large-scale functional brain networks in the field of cognitive neuroscience. However, there is inconsistency across studies in both nomenclature and the functional entities being described. There is a need for a unifying framework that standardizes terminology across studies while also bringing analyses and results into the same reference space. Here we improve the accessibility of a previously developed whole-brain template of canonical functional brain networks, expanding it into a powerful atlas, by manually labeling, organizing, and describing these networks with terms familiar to the fields of cognitive and affective neuroscience. These data-driven functional networks were developed by utilizing more than 100,000 resting-state fMRI datasets and are highly replicable across individual subjects and datasets and capture information from multiple spatial scales. The current report seeks to help optimize the utility of this atlas in future neuroimaging analyses by enhancing the comparability and easing the interpretation of new findings. The benefits of this atlas are not limited to future template-based or reference-guided analyses, but also extend to other data-driven neuroimaging approaches across modalities, such as those using blind independent component analysis (ICA). Future studies utilizing this atlas will contribute to greater harmonization and standardization in functional neuroimaging research.

Cognitive control networks in human and macaque
item.author: Valentina Mione
item.content:encoded: A much-replicated finding in human brain imaging is a distributed ‘multiple-demand’ or MD system, increasing in activity for many kinds of cognitive demand, and centrally involved in cognitive control. MD regions are proposed to encode a distributed mental model of critical task events, bound together in the roles and relationships needed to direct action selection. Though previous data hint at a corresponding network in the macaque, there has been no direct comparison to human data. Here we used functional magnetic resonance imaging to measure whole-brain activation in a multi-step saccadic maze task, compared to a control requiring similar moves but without goal-based decisions. Human data were a close match to the canonical MD network, extended to include adjacent regions, and in particular much of the canonical dorsal attention network. Data from two monkeys suggested correspondences in dorsomedial frontal, insula/orbitofrontal, and posterior temporal cortex. In lateral frontal cortex, there was just a single, largely dorsal activation patch, in contrast to multiple distinct human patches. In one animal, as in humans, there was accompanying activation of dorsal and medial parietal cortex. In macaques, as in humans, together with previous data, our findings suggest an extended and strongly interconnected brain network recruited by increased cognitive challenge.

item.title: Blood-derived dietary protein promotes sleep in the mosquito Aedes aegypti
item.author: Zach N Adelman
item.content:encoded: Sleep is a ubiquitous, yet highly variable, behavior across species. The duration and timing of sleep are influenced by ecological demands and dietary context. In the mosquito , a blood-feeding insect with specialized nutritional requirements, the relationship between feeding and sleep remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated how blood-derived dietary protein influences sleep regulation. Using postural analysis, videography, and arousal-threshold assays, we established that immobility bouts of ≥10 min reliably define sleep in . Mosquitoes lacking the circadian clock gene still maintained daily sleep rhythms but exhibited reduced sleep duration and heightened overall activity. Infrared activity monitoring revealed that blood-fed females showed a marked increase in sleep beginning immediately after feeding and persisting for several days, accompanied by reduced locomotor activity. Notably, this sleep elevation lasted well beyond the cessation of previously reported host-seeking phases, raising the possibility of distinct phases of opportunistic vs. targeted host pursuit. To determine the dietary basis of this effect, we tested mosquitoes fed a bovine serum albumin (BSA)-based diet. BSA feeding alone was sufficient to mimic the sleep-promoting and activity-reducing effects of blood, suggesting dietary protein is a major nutritional regulator. Moreover, RNAi-mediated knockdown of the leucokinin receptor (), which has previously been associated with fluid homeostasis and feeding behavior, resulted in enhanced sleep and reduced activity, implicating mosquito LK signaling in the modulation of postprandial sleep. Together, these findings demonstrate that blood-derived proteins drive sustained increases in sleep and reductions in locomotor activity in . This work positions as a model for dissecting nutrient-specific regulation of sleep and highlights potential adaptive functions of protein-induced quiescence, such as energy conservation and predator avoidance. More broadly, it provides insight into how specialized diets shape the neural and behavioral architecture of sleep.

item.title: Ramping-up hippocampal ripples and their neocortical coupling support human visual short-term memory
item.author: Ying Cai
item.content:encoded: Emerging evidence suggests that the hippocampus contributes to visual short-term memory (VSTM). However, the neural mechanisms through which hippocampal activity supports the maintenance of VSTM representations remain largely unknown. Here, using intracranial EEG recordings from human participants performing a delayed match-to-sample task for naturalistic objects, we investigated the role of hippocampal ripple activity—brief high-frequency oscillations associated with memory replay—in VSTM maintenance and hippocampal-neocortical communication. We found that hippocampal ripple rates progressively ramped up during the maintenance period and supported successful VSTM. More critically, hippocampal ripples were temporally coupled with the ripples in the lateral temporal lobe (LTL), and these coupled ripples were associated with memory reactivation in the LTL. These findings provide direct evidence that hippocampal–neocortical interaction via coupled ripples supports VSTM, extending the role of hippocampal ripples from long-term consolidation to short-term mnemonic processes and offering new insights into the dynamic coding mechanisms of working memory.

item.content:encoded: The endogenous opioid system regulates reward and aversion through multiple peptides and receptor subtypes distributed across the brain. In this review, we focus on two opioids: enkephalins, classically linked to reward, and dynorphins, classically linked to aversion. We argue that this dichotomy oversimplifies a system defined by circuit specificity and context dependence. Methodological advances have enabled direct measurement and manipulation of endogenous opioid signaling in vivo at behaviorally relevant timescales, and evidence shows that endogenous opioid signaling is temporally dynamic, circuit-specific, and functionally heterogeneous, challenging simple reward-versus-aversion models. We discuss how these advances reshape our understanding of dynorphin and enkephalin function, using the nucleus accumbens–ventral pallidum–ventral tegmental area circuit as a framework, given its dense, interacting opioid systems and a central role in rewarding and aversive behaviors.

Here, we show that inhibiting CCL5 using antibodies or not only reduced infarct area and preserved neurological function in MCAO mice but also attenuated astrocyte reactivity and microglial activation, protected dendritic structures, and maintained spine density. Consistent with these findings, the application of Maraviroc, a CCR5 antagonist, reduced infarct size, decreased neuronal apoptosis, and upregulated the ERK/CREB pathway in neurons treated with OGD. item.title: Neurotransmitter and Transcriptomic Basis of Gray Matter Volume Abnormalities in Alzheimer's Disease: A Meta‐Analysis
item.author: Kuanrong Jian, Pengfei Zhang, Haoran Xu, Wenxiong Liu, Yuanyuan Li, Graham J. Kemp, Qiyong Gong
item.content:encoded: This meta-analysis maps convergent gray matter atrophy in Alzheimer's disease and interprets it across brain networks, neurotransmitter systems, and transcriptomic profiles, highlighting multilevel neurobiological mechanisms underlying AD-related structural degeneration.Alzheimer's disease (AD), the commonest neurodegenerative disorder, is characterized by progressive cognitive decline. However, much remains unclear about brain morphological alterations in AD and the underlying molecular mechanisms. We conducted a whole-brain voxel-wise meta-analysis using Seed-based d Mapping with Permutation of Subject Images to identify consistent gray matter volume (GMV) alterations in AD. Significant clusters were assigned to AAL regions and Yeo 7 functional networks and further annotated via Neurosynth. Spatial correspondence between the meta-analysis results and 29 neurotransmitter maps was assessed with JuSpace. Transcriptional associations were assessed using Allen Human Brain Atlas data with partial least squares regression and gene enrichment analysis. The meta-analysis included 70 voxel-based morphometry studies, reporting 2628 AD patients and 2508 healthy controls. AD patients had lower GMV than controls in the bilateral hippocampus, bilateral parahippocampal gyrus and bilateral amygdala ( < 0.05, FWE corrected), regions mainly involved in the default mode network, ventral attention network and the limbic network. Sensitivity analyses indicated high robustness, with low heterogeneity. Neurosynth decoding found the regions of lower GMV to be related to emotional processing and facial expression recognition. Neurotransmitter mapping revealed multiple spatial correlations, notably with the dopaminergic and serotonergic systems ( < 0.001, FDR corrected). Genes associated with the lower-GMV regions were enriched mainly in cytoplasmic translation, ribosomal subunits, cadherin-mediated cell adhesion, and ligand-gated ion channel activity. These findings suggest that GMV alterations in AD predominantly affect temporal regions within specific functional networks and are associated with neurotransmitter systems and molecular pathways.

item.title: Electrophysiological “Brain Power” Dissipation: MEG Model‐Dependent Power Estimates and Regional Metabolic Correlates
item.author: Vikram Nathan, Malte Hoeltershinken, Eleanor Hill, Carsten H. Wolters, Sylvain Baillet
item.content:encoded: We calculate power (P) dissipated by MEG-visible currents, a novel metric distinct from metabolic cost. Sensitivity analyzes and order-of-magnitude checks suggest methodological choices for current and resistance could shift estimates by 1–2 orders of magnitude. We then correlate this dipole P metric against whole-brain oxygen and ketone metabolism maps, revealing spatial correspondences.The human brain is often described as remarkably energy efficient, with its metabolic power consumption estimated at approximately 20 watts (W). Biophysical models partition this metabolic budget across cellular processes, including neuronal signaling. However, the electrical power dissipated by the synchronized cortical activity measurable with noninvasive electrophysiology remains unknown and should not be equated with total cortical energetic demand. Here, we used magnetoencephalography (MEG) source imaging of resting-state activity to estimate electrical power dissipation in cortical gray matter. Across 30 participants, mean total primary power summed over the modeled cortical source space was 6.6 × 10 W. We interpret this value as an empirical, model-dependent power estimate for the synchronized component of cortical activity accessible to MEG, rather than as an estimate of total cortical power. Targ‑eted sensitivity analyzes and order-of-magnitude checks suggested that the tested methodological choices could shift the estimate by approximately one to two orders of magnitude, but not enough to bridge the gap with metabolic benchmarks. Under a magnitude-based root-mean-squares approximation, finite-element estimates of secondary-current dissipation were approximately 30% of primary power in four central-tendency exemplars. Spatial patterns of MEG-derived power showed associations with PET-derived oxygen metabolism and transcriptomic maps of ketone metabolism, with heterogeneous effects across functional networks. These results define the scope and limitations of MEG-derived electrophysiological power estimates and motivate multiscale models linking synchronized electrical activity to regional metabolism.

item.title: Data‐Driven EEG‐fMRI Fusion: From Multimodal Integration to Latent Neural Inference
item.author: Souvik Phadikar, Xinhui Li, Eloy Geenjaar, Reihaneh Hassanzadeh, Lei Wu, Mahshid Fouladivanda, Brad Baker, Vince D. Calhoun
item.content:encoded: This in-depth methodological review systematically examines data-driven EEG-fMRI fusion frameworks, including ICA-, CCA-, tensor-, and deep learning-based approaches, highlighting their core assumptions, advantages, limitations, and applications. The review further discusses key challenges, evaluation strategies, and emerging directions to guide selection of appropriate fusion methods for specific neuroscientific and clinical questions.Simultaneous electroencephalography (EEG) and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) capture neural dynamics across complementary temporal and spatial scales, but analyzing them jointly is difficult: the two modalities differ in measurement mechanisms, temporal resolution, and neurovascular coupling. EEG-fMRI fusion can be framed as an inverse problem, where the goal is to recover latent neural processes only partially observed through electrophysiological and hemodynamic signals. Here, we review data-driven fusion methods published between 2000 and 2025, focusing on techniques that identify shared neural representations across modalities. We organize methods by fusion strategies (symmetric vs. asymmetric), methodological objectives (factorization vs. translation), and modeling assumptions (linear vs. nonlinear), and discuss evaluation metrics and visualization strategies in current use. A recurring finding is the absence of a universal validation standard and the difficulty of interpreting latent multimodal components. Across neurological, psychiatric, and cognitive applications, EEG-fMRI fusion has revealed distributed network dynamics not accessible through unimodal analyses, though temporal misalignment, noise-induced coupling, and model-dependent interpretation remain persistent challenges. We close by discussing directions including nonlinear modeling, flexible coupling frameworks, and large-scale group-level fusion, and situate the field within a broader view of EEG-fMRI fusion as a problem of latent neural inference.

item.title: Perceptual glimpses are locally accumulated and globally maintained at distinct processing levels
item.author: Simon P Kelly
item.content:encoded: Making decisions often requires the integration of multiple pieces of information. An extensive body of research has investigated the neural architecture underpinning evidence accumulation in perceptual tasks where information is continuously present, but less is known about how this neural architecture operates in situations affording only intermittent glimpses of an evidence source. In two electroencephalography experiments, human participants judged the direction of up to two pulses of motion evidence separated by gaps of varying duration. Our behavioural analysis found that participants used both pulses but underutilised the second and showed no systematic decrease in accuracy as a function of gap duration. At the neural level, motor beta lateralisation tracked cumulative evidence across pulses, maintaining a sustained representation of the decision variable through the gap and until response. In contrast, the centroparietal positivity (CPP), a previously characterised signature of evidence accumulation, built up transiently to a peak that scaled with each pulse’s contribution to the decision variable (i.e. the absolute belief update it produced), falling back to baseline in between pulses. These patterns were recapitulated in a model where pulse-information transiently integrated at the CPP level is fed to and maintained at a bounded motor level. In this model, the evidence in the second pulse is only integrated to the extent that the evidence in the first pulse falls short of the bound, or not integrated at all if a bound has already been hit.

item.title: Rhodopsin 7 is an ancestral non-canonical photoreceptor that shapes light-responsive behavior
item.author: Valentina Kirsch
item.content:encoded: Animals rely on light not only for vision but also to adapt behavior to their environment through non-image-forming pathways. In , most rhodopsins mediate retinal image formation, but Rhodopsin 7 (RH7) is widely expressed in the brain and optic lobe, acting as a non-canonical light sensor reminiscent of mammalian melanopsin. We combined expression mapping, behavioral assays, and phylogenetic comparisons to investigate its function. RH7 detects temporal changes in luminance, guiding rapid behavioral responses, and regulating daily activity patterns. Flies lacking RH7 are less active during the dark phase, while strains with constitutively active RH7 show increased activity. Phylogenetic analyses suggest that RH7 is an ancient rhodopsin present across panarthropods, representing an intermediate between G protein–coupled receptors and specialized rhodopsins, highlighting a key step in the evolution of non-visual light perception. These findings show that RH7 functions as a melanopsin-like sensor, shaping behavior, and illuminating the origins of light detection.

item.title: Transposons contribute to splice-isoform diversity in the Drosophila brain
item.author: Tina Rainey
item.content:encoded: The extraordinary complexity of the brain depends in part on the vast diversity of mRNA isoforms it expresses, often in a cell-type specific manner. In a recent study, we found that intronic transposable elements (TEs) are spliced into neural transcripts and diversify the splice isoform repertoire of neurons and glia (Treiber and Waddell, 2020). A recent paper by Azad et al. revisits these findings using their TIDAL analysis pipeline applied to our published data (Azad et al., 2024). Their analysis did not find any of the splicing reads we reported and although they used RT-PCR to test seven of the 264 TE–gene pairs we had previously reported, they failed to validate TE–gene splicing in any of them. Here, we conduct a quantitative analysis of TE exonisation and show that intronic TE insertions are frequently recruited as alternative exons, with exon usage ranging from rare events to near-complete inclusion in transcripts. We implement this analysis in an improved version of our TEChim software and present clear support for TE–gene splicing at the seven loci tested by Azad et al. We also identify methodological issues in the experimental and computational design of the Azad et al. study that likely explains their failure to detect TE–gene chimeras, while demonstrating that TE–gene splicing can be detected by RT-PCR under appropriate experimental conditions. Together, our data demonstrates that TE splice isoforms are not rare artefacts but measurable and biologically relevant features of the brain transcriptome that may contribute to the molecular complexity and functional adaptability of the brain.

item.title: Hierarchical neural circuit theory of normalization and inter-areal communication
item.author: Stefano Martiniani
item.content:encoded: The primate brain exhibits a hierarchical, modular architecture with conserved microcircuits executing canonical computations across reciprocally connected cortical areas. We present a hierarchical neural circuit theory with feedback connections that dynamically implements divisive normalization across its hierarchy. In a two-stage instantiation (V1 ↔ V2), increasing feedback from V2 to V1 amplifies responses in both areas. We analytically derive power spectra (V1) and coherence spectra (V1-V2) as functions of frequency () and compare them with experimental observations: peaks in both spectra shift to higher frequencies with increased stimulus contrast, and power decays as 1/ at high frequencies. The closed-form spectra are validated against direct stochastic simulation of the full nonlinear circuit across contrasts. The theory further predicts distinctive spectral signatures of feedback and input gain modulation. Crucially, the theory offers a unified view of inter-areal communication, defined as the ability to linearly predict neural activity in one brain area from neural activity in another, with emergent features consistent with empirical observations of both communication subspaces and inter-areal coherence. It admits a low-dimensional communication subspace, where inter-areal communication is lower-dimensional than within-area communication. It further predicts that: (1) increasing feedback strength enhances inter-areal communication and diminishes within-area communication, without altering the subspace dimensionality; (2) communication is strongest, and the subspace dimensionality lowest, at the frequencies at which V1-V2 coherence peaks; (3) normalization reduces the subspace dimensionality. Finally, a three-area (V1 ↔ V4 and V1 ↔ V5) instantiation of the theory demonstrates that differential feedback from higher to lower cortical areas dictates their dynamic functional connectivity. Altogether, our theory provides a robust and analytically tractable framework for generating experimentally testable predictions about normalization, inter-areal communication, and functional connectivity.

item.author: Volodymyr I Dzhala
item.content:encoded: Seizures upregulate Na-K–2Cl (NKCC1)-mediated Cl influx and downregulate K-Cl (KCC2)-mediated Cl efflux via the WNK-SPAK/OSR1 kinases, leading to cytoplasmic chloride ([Cl]) accumulation, reduced GABAergic inhibition, and anticonvulsant failure. Early studies found that inhibiting WNK-kinase reduced baseline [Cl] (E) and seizures via increased KCC2 activity. However, increased KCC2 activity alone should not affect E, whose determinants are more complex. We determined the net effects of the WNK-SPAK/OSR1 pathway inhibitor WNK463 on E and [Cl] transients during spontaneous ictal-like discharges (ILDs) in organotypic hippocampal slice cultures from mice. Pharmacological inhibition and targeted siRNA silencing demonstrated that the anti-ictal effects of WNK463 involved both NKCC1 and KCC2. Our data support a mechanism whereby mutual NKCC1 inhibition and KCC2 activation via the WNK-SPAK/OSR1 pathway exert powerful anti-ictal effects by facilitating [Cl] extrusion during ILDs.

item.title: Emotional valence experiences, not sensory valence: Clarifying James’s theory of emotion: Reply to Roelofs (2026).
item.content:encoded: Roelofs (2026) argues that our findings, showing that pleasant and unpleasant feelings follow Weber’s law, do not support William James’s theory of emotion because James excluded such feelings from his account. We address this claim by offering two clarifications. First, we argue that this conclusion rests on a mismatch between James’s terminology and the terms as used in contemporary affective science. While James excluded (un)pleasant feelings from his theory, he excluded basic (un)pleasant affective qualities perceived as inherent properties of the stimulus itself, what he termed “tone of feeling,” but he did not exclude valence experiences. What distinguishes between the two levels are the objects, for example, “this picture is ugly” (tone of feeling) versus “this picture makes me feel unpleasant” (valence experiences). In our experiments, participants reported about their (un)pleasant emotional state. This corresponds to what James conceptualized as a “felt state of excitement,” an intense subjective state attributed to the experiencer that he explicitly identified as the defining feature of emotion rather than excluding it. Second, we clarify that our reference to James was intended to situate our findings within the broader historical tradition of perceptual theories of emotion rather than to support the specific details of his original account. Ultimately, once the terminology is aligned, it becomes clear that our results are entirely consistent with James’s framework. In fact, they provide modern empirical support for his core vision: that emotions are, at their essence, perceptual processes. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved)

item.title: Weber’s law in feelings does not support James’s theory of emotions: Commentary on Berkovich and Meiran (2023, 2024).
item.content:encoded: Using an evidence-accumulation model of feeling generation to analyze manual responses, Berkovich and Meiran (2023, 2024) observed that feelings of pleasure and displeasure evoked by stimuli follow Weber’s law (Weber, 1834, 1846). They regarded this finding as strong support, and perhaps the strongest yet, for James’s (1884) theory of emotions, according to which emotions are sensory experiences of bodily changes. Here, I argue that Weber’s law in feelings cannot, strictly speaking, support James’s sensory theory, simply because he excluded feelings of pleasure and displeasure from his theory. James (1894) made this particularly clear in response to Lehmann (1892), who observed that the bodily change (i.e., change in heartbeat and respiration) evoked by stimuli developed after the feeling of pleasure or displeasure was reported, and that therefore the experience of the change could not be the feeling. In modern physiological studies, central indicators of pleasure and displeasure have also been found to precede peripheral bodily changes. Furthermore, the primary interoceptive and proprioceptive brain areas were not found to be activated during pleasure and displeasure, compared to a neutral state. So even if we were to extend James’s theory to feelings of pleasure and displeasure, Berkovich and Meiran’s findings, in the absence of physiological evidence to the contrary, would not support the theory. item.title: Interdependent conditions for successful human–AI delegation

item.content:encoded: People increasingly rely on AI systems for consequential tasks, from clinical diagnosis to software development. The gains are real yet difficult to realize reliably. We identify four psychological and structural conditions for successful delegation: accurate human assessment of AI capabilities, calibrated AI uncertainty communication, sustained human monitoring capacity, and compatible task structure. Each condition is well-studied, yet we propose that they form an interdependent system in which each one’s effectiveness depends on the state of the others. Because these dependencies are bidirectional, we suggest that they can compound over time into virtuous cycles or cascading degradation, and that improving any single condition can fail or shift the bottleneck. item.title: Learning-associated flexibility of cortical taste coding is impaired in Shank3 knockout mice
item.author: Gina G Turrigiano
item.content:encoded: The ability to update the valence of sensory perception to influence behavior is crucial for survival. A common phenotype in autism spectrum disorders (ASDs) is defects in sensory processing, but whether these defects impair flexible sensory encoding is largely unexplored. In particular, how genetic risk factors such as deletion affect the adaptability of cortical taste processing and downstream behavior is unknown. To address this gap, we performed two-photon calcium imaging during a conditioned taste aversion (CTA) learning paradigm, an ethologically relevant form of associative learning that depends on taste processing in the gustatory cortex (GC), to examine how knockout alters taste-related neuronal activity in GC and influences CTA learning. We found that GC neurons in knockout mice exhibited reduced stimulus-evoked suppression and increased trial-to-trial correlated variability during the acquisition of CTA memory. These activity changes, which likely reduced signal-to-noise ratio in GC, were associated with slower CTA acquisition in knockout mice. In both genotypes, CTA learning enhanced, while subsequent extinction reduced, taste discriminability in GC, and both extinction and the associated reduction in discriminability were faster in knockout than in wild-type mice. Together, these results show that loss is associated with destabilized cortical activity dynamics in GC, which may contribute to inefficient encoding and maintenance of learned taste aversion. These findings show that loss of compromises the ability of animals to update behavior to incorporate negative outcomes, and suggest this loss of flexibility may be an important feature of monogenic ASDs.

item.title: Synthetic torpor in the rat protects the heart from ischaemia-reperfusion injury
item.author: Una R Wilcox
item.content:encoded: During times of environmental stress, many animals enter torpor: a reversible protective physiological state typically characterised by reductions in core temperature, heart rate, and oxygen consumption. Species that naturally enter this hypothermic and hypometabolic state are tolerant of ischaemia-reperfusion injury. Consequently, there is a growing interest in utilising aspects of torpor for clinical applications such as protection from stroke or myocardial infarction. It is currently unknown, however, whether a torpor-like state is protective in animals that do not naturally enter torpor. Using viral vector-mediated chemogenetic activation of the medial preoptic area of the hypothalamus, we induced synthetic torpor in the rat, a species that does not naturally enter torpor. We demonstrate this state is cardioprotective in an ex vivo ischaemia-reperfusion injury model with an ~40% reduction in infarct size. Synthetic torpor-induced cardioprotection of the normothermic, isolated heart is not dependent on prior hypothermia in vivo. Phosphoproteomic analysis of cardiac tissue indicates that the protective effects of synthetic torpor may be mediated by parallel activation of cell survival and stress tolerance pathways and inhibition of cell death pathways. These findings provide important insights into the mechanisms of organ protective effects of synthetic torpor states with implications for future clinical translation in humans.

item.title: Cholinergic blockade reveals a role for human hippocampal theta in memory encoding but not retrieval
item.author: Tamara Gedankien
item.content:encoded: Cholinergic dysfunction is a hallmark of Alzheimer’s disease and other memory disorders. Yet, the neurophysiological mechanisms linking cholinergic signaling to memory remain poorly understood. In this study, we administered scopolamine, a muscarinic cholinergic antagonist, to neurosurgical patients with intracranial electrodes as they performed an associative recognition memory task. When scopolamine was present at encoding, we observed disruptions to hippocampal slow theta oscillations (2–4 Hz), with selective impairments to recollection-based memory. However, when scopolamine was present during retrieval alone, we observed disruptions to slow theta without impaired memory performance. These disruptions included dose-dependent reductions in theta power, theta phase reset, and encoding–retrieval pattern reinstatement. Together, our results challenge the notion that theta oscillations are necessary for memory retrieval, and instead suggest that theta universally reflects an encoding-related neural state. These findings motivate updates to current models of acetylcholine’s role in memory and may inform future therapies targeting rhythmic biomarkers of memory dysfunction.

item.title: Functional brain signatures of successful cognitive aging
item.author: Niklas Behrenbruch, Larissa Fischer, Hans Kirschner, Theresa M. Harrison, Anne Maass
item.content:encoded: Cognitive aging trajectories vary markedly. While many older adults experience gradual decline in memory and executive function, some maintain high cognitive performance well into advanced age. Understanding the neural mechanisms underlying this variability carries important implications for early detection of unfavorable aging trajectories and the development of interventions. Here, we review functional brain signatures associated with successful cognitive aging in humans, integrating evidence from functional magnetic resonance imaging and electroencephalography within a unified conceptual framework of brain maintenance and compensation. Across both modalities, evidence increasingly links successful cognitive aging to the preservation of youth-like neural dynamics, while the contribution of compensatory neural recruitment remains empirically contested and methodologically difficult to establish.

item.title: Midbrain somatostatin-expressing cells control pain-suppression during defensive states
item.author: Zoe Grivet
item.content:encoded: In threatening situations, animals exhibit a broad range of behavioral and autonomic responses. As such, a crucial adaptive response is the inhibition of pain, which facilitates relevant defensive behaviors that promote survival. Whereas the structures and mechanisms involved in fear and pain behaviors are well documented, little is known about the precise neuronal mechanisms mediating the emotional regulation of endogenous pain-suppression. Here, we used a combination of behavioral, anatomical, optogenetic, and electrophysiological approaches to investigate, in male mice, the role of somatostatin-expressing cells in the ventrolateral periaqueductal gray matter (SST vlPAG cells) in the control of analgesia induced during defensive states. Our data indicate that optogenetic inhibition of SST vlPAG cells promotes analgesia irrespective of animal defensive state. In contrast, optogenetic activation of long-range SST vlPAG cells that project to the rostral ventromedial medulla (RVM) abolishes the analgesia mediated by fear behavior. Together, these results identify a novel circuit mechanism composed of long-range SST vlPAG cells projecting to the RVM that regulate analgesia elicited during defensive states.

item.title: Dual-feature selectivity enables bidirectional coding in visual cortical neurons
item.author: Tori Shinn
item.content:encoded: Sensory neurons are traditionally viewed as feature detectors that respond with an increase in firing rate to preferred stimuli while remaining unresponsive to others. Here, we identify a dual-feature encoding strategy in macaque visual cortex, wherein many neurons in areas V1 and V4 are selectively tuned to two distinct visual features—one that enhances and one that suppresses activity—around an elevated baseline firing rate. By combining neuronal recordings with functional digital twin models—deep learning-based predictive models of biological neurons—we were able to systematically identify each neuron’s preferred and non-preferred features. These feature pairs served as anchors for a continuous, low-dimensional axis in natural image similarity space, along which neuronal activity varied approximately linearly. Within a single visual area, visual features that strongly or weakly activated individual neurons also had a high probability of modulating the activity of other neurons, suggesting a shared feature selectivity across the population that structures stimulus encoding. We show that this encoding strategy is conserved across species, present in both primary and lateral visual areas of mouse cortex. Dual-feature selectivity is consistent with recent anatomical evidence for feature-specific inhibitory connectivity, complementing the feature-detector principle through circuit mechanisms in which selective excitation and inhibition may together enhance the representational capacity of the neuronal population.

Building on early psychophysiological studies, the field has expanded substantially since the mid-2000s through an increasing range of methods and models. We highlight that its strength lies in spanning multiple levels of analysis to address marketing-relevant questions. We highlight four major trends driving the field: improving behavioral prediction, synthesizing evidence through multidataset analyses, developing formal models linking neural processes to consumer decision-making, and integrating brain and body measures. Together, these advances position consumer neuroscience as an integrative science with implications for marketing, policy, and consumer welfare.

item.title: Constructing events across perception, action, and thought
item.author: Dasom Kwon, Jiwoong Park, Won Mok Shim
item.content:encoded: The brain organizes continuous experience into events that structure episodic memory and guide behavior. Traditional accounts have primarily focused on sensory discontinuities and prediction errors that trigger updates of event models. Here, we broaden this view to consider event boundaries arising during goal-directed behavior, spontaneous thought, and memory recall, including transitions generated in the absence of corresponding changes in sensory input. We propose that prediction error and uncertainty provide complementary signals for event model updating: prediction errors signal a violation of current expectations, whereas uncertainty may promote updating when upcoming states become difficult to predict. We further suggest that the hippocampus may serve as a candidate hub linking boundary-related representational changes across perception, action, and thought. Together, this framework offers an integrative account of how the brain detects and generates event structure in continuous experience to support memory and behavior.

item.title: The resource elasticity of control
item.author: Levi Solomyak
item.content:encoded: The ability to determine how much the environment can be controlled through our actions has long been viewed as fundamental to adaptive behavior. While traditional accounts treat controllability as a fixed property of the environment, we argue that real-world controllability often depends on the effort, time, and money we are able and willing to invest. In such cases, controllability can be said to be to invested resources. Here, we propose that inferring this elasticity is essential for efficient resource allocation, and thus, elasticity misestimations result in maladaptive behavior. To test this hypothesis, we developed a novel treasure hunt game where participants encountered environments with varying degrees of controllability and elasticity. Across two pre-registered studies (=514), we first demonstrate that people infer elasticity and adapt their resource allocation accordingly. We then present a computational model that explains how people make this inference and identify individual elasticity biases that lead to suboptimal resource allocation. Finally, we show that overestimation of elasticity is associated with elevated psychopathology involving an impaired sense of control. These findings establish the elasticity of control as a distinct cognitive construct guiding adaptive behavior and a computational marker for control-related maladaptive behavior.

item.title: Expectation-driven gain modulation of preparatory spatial attention
item.author: Stefan van der Stigchel
item.content:encoded: The visual system can flexibly adjust attentional deployment to match task demands, but whether observers can proactively modulate the spatial scope of attention based on expectations about upcoming search difficulty remains unclear. According to the zoom lens model, attention can narrow or broaden its spatial extent, with narrower focus enhancing processing efficiency, a mechanism that would benefit target discrimination in crowded displays. We tested whether observers adjust attentional scope when expecting sparse versus dense search arrays by combining spatial cueing with block-wise manipulations of display density expectations. Participants performed a visual search task in which endogenous cues predicted target location, while blocks predominantly contained either sparse (1 target, 3 distractors) or dense (1 target, 7 distractors) displays. We applied inverted encoding models to broadband EEG data to reconstruct spatial channel tuning functions, enabling precise characterization of both the locus and breadth of attentional deployment. Behaviorally, expecting difficult searches selectively improved accuracy at cued locations without costs elsewhere. Consistent with this selective benefit, neural measurements revealed that expectancy enhanced the amplitude of spatially selective responses at the attended location but did not alter tuning width. These findings demonstrate that expectations about search difficulty modulate attention through gain-based signal enhancement rather than adjustments to spatial scope, revealing that preparatory attentional control operates via amplitude modulation within a stable spatial focus. This mechanism complements reactive attentional adjustments and provides an efficient means for the visual system to optimize processing under predictable task demands.

item.title: Simple methods to acutely measure multiple timing metrics among the sexual repertoire of male Drosophila
item.author: Yutong Song
item.content:encoded: Male courtship behavior is a key model for studying temporal decision-making. While courtship index (CI) is widely used to quantify mating activity, other timing metrics like courtship latency, copulation latency (CL), and mating duration (MD) remain understudied. Traditional methods for quantifying these behaviors are often labor-intensive and prone to human error. In this study, we present a protocol combining a modular chamber system and automated software (DrosoMating) to quantify six key timing metrics during male courtship. Our image-based video analysis enables precise identification of courtship and copulation events, as well as quantification of their timing and duration under controlled conditions. Validation shows <0.05% error rates and 98–99% agreement with manual scoring for CL, CI, and MD. The protocol supports genetic and neural circuit manipulations, detecting subtle genetic, social, and environmental behavioral variations. By minimizing manual effort and standardizing data collection, this approach facilitates scalable, reproducible studies on adaptive trade-offs, learning, and neural mechanisms in mating behavior. This method streamlines timing analysis in male courtship, offering reproducible metrics for behavioral genetics.

item.title: The hypoxic response extends lifespan through a bioaminergic and peptidergic neural circuit
item.author: Shijiao Huang
item.content:encoded: A coordinated response to stress is crucial for promoting the short- and long-term health of an organism. The perception of stress, frequently through the nervous system, can lead to physiological changes that are fundamental to maintaining homeostasis. Activating the response to low oxygen, or hypoxia, extends healthspan and lifespan in . However, despite some positive impacts, negative effects of the hypoxic response in specific tissues prevent translation of their benefits in mammals. Thus, it is imperative to identify which components of this response promote longevity. Here, we interrogate the cell-nonautonomous signaling pathway downstream of genetic activation of the hypoxic response. We find that HIF-1-mediated signaling in ADF serotonergic neurons is both necessary and sufficient for lifespan extension. Signaling through the serotonin receptor SER-7 in the GABAergic RIS interneurons is necessary in this process. Our findings also highlight the involvement of additional neural signaling molecules, including the neurotransmitters tyramine and GABA, and the neuropeptide NLP-17, in mediating longevity effects. Finally, we demonstrate that oxygen- and carbon-dioxide-sensing neurons act downstream of HIF-1 in this circuit. Together, these insights demonstrate a circuit for how genetic induction of the hypoxic response cell-nonautonomously modifies aging and suggests valuable targets for modulating aging in mammals.

item.title: Distinct neural representations of perceptual and numerical absence in the human brain
item.author: Stephen M Fleming
item.content:encoded: The ability to represent absences is fundamental to human perception and cognition. Sensitivity to non-numerical absences depends on inferring a lack of sensory evidence, enabling the recognition of a lack of environmental resources or other objects. In turn, encoding numerical absence as a concept – in the form of the number zero – has enabled a multitude of technological and mathematical advances. Whether perceptual and conceptual absences rely on overlapping or distinct neural representations in the human brain, however, remains unknown. We employed three different tasks together with magnetoencephalography to characterise neural representations of absence evoked within perceptual and numerical domains. Using multivariate decoding and Bayes factor analyses, we replicate previous findings of shared representations of numerical absence across symbolic and non-symbolic formats. In contrast, we show that these representations of numerical absence are distinct from those evoked by non-numerical absences. This result held even after controlling for stimulus-level confounds which generate surface-level similarities between perceptual absences and non-symbolic empty sets. Our results extend a boundary between perception and cognition to the domain of absence and provide insight into the different mechanisms employed by the human brain to both perceive and conceive of absences.

item.title: Spectraplakin is required for dendritic microtubule organization via a tip-based mechanism in Drosophila
item.author: Yitao Shen
item.content:encoded: The differential microtubule organization in axons and dendrites underlies neuronal polarity and developmental processes, like neurite pruning. How neurons achieve their specific microtubule organization during development is an area of active research, and it has been especially hard to explain how dendritic microtubules are oriented with their plus ends toward the soma. Transient microtubule nucleation from tips of early growing dendrites has been proposed as a mechanism that would explain how this orientation is set up. In a survey for cytoskeletal regulators involved in dendrite pruning and microtubule organization in , we found the spectraplakin Short stop (Shot), an actin/microtubule crosslinker. Loss of Shot causes microtubule orientation defects already during early dendrite development, when Shot is transiently recruited to tips of growing dendrites via its actin-binding domain. Genetic and functional evidence suggests that Shot’s primary function in this process is to locally stabilize microtubules. We also provide evidence for an independent, developmentally transient microtubule nucleation mechanism. Our data highlight the importance of transient and localized microtubule regulation for dendritic microtubule organization.

item.title: Dopaminergic neurons linking threat processing to cardiac modulation and locomotor responses
item.author: Yuki Uemura
item.content:encoded: Heartbeat and behavior are tightly coordinated during defensive states, yet the neuronal mechanisms linking threat processing to cardiac modulation—and the potential contribution of cardiac dynamics to behavioral output—remain poorly understood. Here, using simultaneous recordings of heartbeat and behavior in tethered , we show that mechanical threat triggers locomotion together with rapid cardiac deceleration. We identify two pairs of dopaminergic neurons, termed DA-WED neurons, that mediate this cardiac response. Silencing these neurons markedly attenuates threat-induced cardiac deceleration, whereas optogenetic activation induces cardiac deceleration in the absence of threat. Two-photon calcium imaging further shows that DA-WED neurons are activated by mechanical threat, and manipulating their activity bidirectionally modulates threat-induced locomotion. Linking cardiac dynamics to behavior, direct optogenetic manipulation of cardiomyocytes that quantitatively reproduces threat-evoked cardiac deceleration is accompanied by increased locomotion. Together, these results identify a dopaminergic descending pathway that links threat processing to cardiac modulation and suggest that cardiac dynamics may contribute to shaping defensive behavior.

item.title: Lost, then found: transient forgetting in humans and machines
item.author: Milan Van Maldegem, Hans Op de Beeck, Niels A. Taatgen, Tinne Tuytelaars, Gido M. van de Ven
item.content:encoded: Forgetting can be permanent or transient. An intriguing, recently described form of transient forgetting (TF) in artificial neural networks is the stability gap: a network that has already learned a first task exhibits transient yet substantial forgetting when it begins additional training on a second task alongside the first. Could an analogous phenomenon be found in humans? Following a literature survey, six types of TF in humans were identified, categorised by their sources: learning, retrieval, spontaneous, overgeneralisation, task-switching, and multitasking. Although all differ in important ways from the stability gap, it is hypothesised that some underlying mechanisms are shared. This opinion article concludes by proposing experiments to test whether a ‘stability gap-like’ form of TF also occurs in humans.

item.title: What can behavior tell us about neural dynamics?
item.author: Fanny Cazettes, Marieke L. Schölvinck
item.content:encoded: For decades, systems neuroscience treated behavior as an endpoint: a simplified output, such as a button press, lick, or saccade, used to isolate neural computations. Richer behavioral measurements have expanded this view by revealing neural dynamics hidden by simple outputs. Yet behavior is not a direct readout of brain activity, because similar behavioral outputs can arise from different neural mechanisms. Interpreting neural dynamics is therefore an inverse problem with no straightforward solution. Behavior can constrain this problem by exposing sensorimotor loops, narrowing plausible explanations for population activity, and formalizing neural–behavioral relationships in joint models. Together, these approaches position behavior as a principled constraint on interpreting neural dynamics and latent cognitive, affective, and computational states.

item.title: Evolving perspectives on cardiac innervation: from relay to a complex regulated network
item.author: Beth A. Habecker, Johanna M. Montgomery
item.content:encoded: Neural control of the heart adjusts cardiac output to the functional demands of the body in order to maintain homeostasis. Sensory afferents monitor blood pressure, metabolites, and other parameters, sending information to the brainstem that then alters the balance of stimulatory sympathetic and inhibitory parasympathetic transmission to the heart. ‘Autonomic imbalance’ between sympathetic and parasympathetic efferent transmission in the heart is a characteristic of cardiovascular and metabolic diseases that contributes to pathology. In this review, we discuss recent studies related to the peripheral components of the cardiac control circuit. We summarize data from induced pluripotent stem cells, small and large animal models, and human studies that reveal more complexity in peripheral components of this system than previously understood. We also discuss peripheral neuroplasticity in cardiovascular disease and the potential impact of neuromodulation therapies.

item.title: A validated antibody toolbox for ALS research
item.author: Zhipeng You
item.content:encoded: A substantial fraction of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)-associated proteins remains poorly characterized, in part because of the limited availability of validated research antibodies. We established knockout (KO)-based antibody characterization workflows and demonstrated that widely used antibodies against the major ALS-associated protein C9orf72 lacked specificity (Laflamme et al., 2019). We subsequently scaled this framework to systematically benchmark research antibodies, revealing that up to 61% fail to perform as recommended by manufacturers (Ayoubi et al., 2023b). Here, we extend this approach by establishing the ALS-Reproducible Antibody Platform (ALS-RAP), a comprehensive effort to generate a publicly available dataset of KO-validated antibodies targeting proteins encoded by ALS risk genes. In total, we characterized 303 antibodies against 33 ALS-associated proteins to identify high-quality reagents for use in western blot, immunoprecipitation, and immunofluorescence. Using these antibodies, we profiled protein levels across human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived and primary neurological cell types. These analyses revealed diverse cellular distributions and higher levels of several ALS-associated proteins in glial populations, consistent with emerging evidence for immune contributions to ALS. Together, ALS-RAP provides a validated antibody toolbox and protein expression resource to support the study of ALS-associated proteins.

item.title: Behavioural and neurogenetic evidence for emotion primitives in the fruit fly Drosophila from an open field test
item.author: Yi Lueningschroer-Wang
item.content:encoded: Emotions are based on evolutionarily conserved building blocks (‘emotion primitives’) that are present across mammals. Whether these building blocks are found in insects is largely undefined. Here, we employ the open field test (OFT) in and focus on wall-following and total walking activity as behavioural indicators of emotion-like states. Wildtype and transgenic flies were subjected to various conditions prior to behavioural testing. The results indicate that wall-following and total walking activity are independent measures that are modulated, with generally increased wall-following observed under aversive stimuli and decreased values under positive conditions, independent of the time of day. The effects of genetic manipulation of selected neuromodulatory systems support their role in modulating emotion-like states in . Activation of reward-related neurons decreased wall-following while inhibition increased it. Moreover, treatment with ethanol or diazepam produced predictable changes in behaviour. Our findings suggest that shares conserved core emotion-like building blocks with vertebrates, and show that wall-following and total walking activity in the OFT can serve as a reliable indicator of emotional valence and arousal in the fruit fly. This positions as a powerful genetic model to dissect the neuronal and neurochemical substrates of emotion primitives.

item.title: THE MOST INFLUENTIAL ARTIST NOBODY KNOWS #history #arthistory #painting #artist #art
item.author: Great Art Explained
item.content:encoded:
Pierre Puvis de Chavannes (1824–1898) was one of the most influential French painters of the nineteenth century, although today he is far less well known than many of the artists he inspired. At a time when Impressionism was transforming painting with its fascination for modern life, light and movement, Puvis looked in an entirely different direction. His paintings depict quiet, dreamlike worlds populated by mysterious figures in timeless landscapes, where very little seems to happen, yet everything feels strangely significant.
Best known for his monumental murals in public buildings, Puvis developed a distinctive style characterised by muted colours, simplified forms, flattened perspectives and an almost complete absence of drama. His figures often appear detached from reality, suspended somewhere between classical antiquity and the modern world.
Although his work might appear conservative today, it was remarkably innovative. By rejecting naturalism in favour of atmosphere, symbolism and emotional suggestion, Puvis helped open the door to modern art. His influence can be traced through Gauguin, Seurat, Matisse and even the young Picasso. He was admired by artists who would go on to challenge almost everything nineteenth-century painting stood for, making him one of the most important, and perhaps most overlooked, bridges between academic tradition and modernism.

item.title: Peripersonal space: a neural system mapping self–environment interaction ‘here and now’
item.author: Andrea Serino
item.content:encoded: The space surrounding the body where physical interactions with external stimuli occur is referred to as peripersonal space (PPS). Traditionally conceived as a spatial construct, PPS is better understood as a neural representation that integrates bodily inputs with external cues to predict body–object interactions. After summarizing its multisensory, motor, and plastic properties, this review draws on computational models to examine how PPS captures statistical regularities of body–object interactions. This predictive function may position PPS as an interface between self and environment, contributing to minimal self-consciousness and its alterations across states of consciousness and neuropsychiatric conditions. Recent findings extend this framework to the inner body, suggesting that interoceptive signals shape PPS and that PPS-related processing may influence immune responses.

item.title: Strength-based organizational approaches facilitate workplace opportunities for people from lower socioeconomic status backgrounds.
item.content:encoded: The workplace stands as one of the most powerful drivers of societal (in)equality. For employees from lower socioeconomic status backgrounds, it can represent both a ticket toward upward mobility and a consequential source of stigma. Four studies build on emerging strength-based research to test whether workplaces can challenge this stigma by creating overarching cultures that recognize the beneficial skills employees gain from their otherwise marginalized identities. Study 1 provided foundational insights into these “strength-based organizational approaches” and their implications for key outcomes derived from the State Authenticity as Fit to Environment model. Employees from lower socioeconomic status backgrounds were especially unlikely to report that their workplaces valued their identities and associated skills, which partially explained subsequent disparities in employees’ broad sense of comfort and efficacy at work. Studies 2a and 2b established these patterns experimentally by demonstrating that exposing participants to a workplace that does communicate a strength-based organizational approach facilitated these professionally productive outcomes while increasing participants’ likelihood of disclosing their marginalized identities within a job application task. Study 3 extended these findings to consider how the approaches may also indirectly expand employees’ equitable access to opportunity through reducing common biases among their supervisors. Randomly assigning workplace supervisors to briefly engage with a company that highlighted the value of employees’ lower socioeconomic status backgrounds increased supervisors’ positive evaluations and likelihood of promoting these employees by 38% relative to an active control condition. Collectively, these preregistered findings illuminate new opportunities to improve workplace functioning and pinpoint the organizational forces underlying person–context interactions. item.title: How we see relations: The case of containment and support.
item.content:encoded: To navigate and act in the environment, it is necessary to recognize objects and the relationships between them. Recognition of objects in visual scenes is rapid and automatic. Are relations between objects in a scene also extracted rapidly and automatically during perception? Here, we considered containment and support, two relations that are fundamental to our understanding of the physical world. Using frequency-tagging electroencephalography on human subjects, we measured stimulus-driven neural responses during rapid visual presentation of images (4 Hz), with a periodic oddball structure to isolate the selective response to object pairs presented side-by-side (e.g., a book and a table) versus two objects in support or containment relations (e.g., a book on a table). We found enhanced responses to objects in support/containment relations (vs. objects side-by-side) when a relation was instantiated by different exemplars of the same scene (e.g., a book on a table), but not by different scenes involving distinct object categories (e.g., a book on a table, a lamp on a stand, a laptop on a desk). These findings indicate that, during scene perception, relations are extracted in a format that generalizes within, but not across, types of visual scenes. We propose that, during perception, relations are not represented as discrete, abstract tokens (“in” or “on”) but rather as objects’ properties, such that changes in the objects entail changes in the relational representation. These results provide new insight into the perceptual foundations of relational processing underlying physical reasoning. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved)

item.title: Task-evoked pupillary responses reveal a role for attentional intensity in auditory discrimination.
item.content:encoded: Sensory discrimination has long been theorized to reflect a core cognitive function underlying intelligence. Building on this tradition, we examined whether task-evoked pupil responses, as an index of mental effort, relate to attention control (AC) and auditory discrimination ability. Using a large data set (N = 336), participants completed three adaptive auditory discrimination tasks (pitch, duration, loudness), a cognitive battery assessing AC, working memory capacity, and fluid intelligence, and pupillometry during task performance. Structural equation modeling confirmed that AC predicted auditory discrimination thresholds and fully mediated the relationship between task-evoked pupil dilation and performance. Trial-level multilevel models revealed that higher task difficulty and errors were associated with larger pupil dilations, especially in demanding tasks. Crucially, individuals with greater AC exhibited steeper increases in pupil dilation with rising task difficulty and were more resilient to performance declines. For high-AC individuals, large pupil responses predicted preserved accuracy; for low-AC individuals, they signaled compensatory effort with diminished success. These results suggest that AC governs both the extent and efficacy of mental effort, determining whether high arousal facilitates or fails to improve performance. This work refines classic resource models by demonstrating that cognitive effort, indexed via pupillometry, supports perception most effectively when guided by strong AC. Findings support a hierarchical model in which AC serves as the functional bridge between arousal, sensory discrimination, and higher order cognition. item.title: The orthographic mind: Orthographic imagery propensity correlates with semantic structure and sensory sensitivity.
item.content:encoded: Individuals differ in their habitual use of internal representational modes, including visual imagery, internal verbalization, and orthographic imagery (the mental simulation of written word forms). The present research examined whether such internal representational propensities relate to semantic organization and external information engagement. Across two studies (total N = 1,399), we assessed individuals’ internal representational modes using the Internal Representations Questionnaire and examined their associations with semantic structure (nine-word semantic rating experiments; N = 1,109) and external information engagement (sensory-processing sensitivity and mobile app usage). Orthographic imagery showed robust associations with both semantic geometry and external information engagement patterns: Individuals with stronger orthographic imagery showed greater cross-category semantic association strength, lower semantic conformity, and lower sensory-processing sensitivity. Internal verbalization was positively associated with within-category semantic cohesion, while visual imagery showed no reliable associations with semantic geometry and limited associations with real-world media engagement. Effects were modest but consistent across experiments. These findings suggest that internal representational modes function as stable weighting biases, subtly modulating semantic geometry and sensory-processing profiles. Such propensities therefore correspond to structured variations in cognition, rather than merely phenomenological differences in inner experience. item.title: Children can suppress salient distractors.
item.content:encoded: From a very young age, our perceptual system is particularly sensitive to salient events. When such events are irrelevant, adults can prevent them from capturing attention by suppressing the salient features and by prioritizing task-relevant information. Previous research suggests that both distractor-suppression and target-prioritization mechanisms are not yet fully developed at ages 5–6. However, this work has not clearly disentangled the two mechanisms. Here, we specifically investigated whether children can suppress the salient feature of an irrelevant distractor. Two groups of children (aged 5–6 and 8–9) searched for a shape-defined target among heterogeneously shaped nontargets. All items had the same color throughout the experiment, but on two thirds of the trials, one item (the singleton distractor) had a unique color that changed at the beginning of each block. We expected this distractor to interfere with search performance during the first half of each block (i.e., when its color was novel). The critical question was whether this interference would be reduced during the second block half (i.e., with enough experience with the distractor’s color). This finding would indicate that the children suppressed the salient distractor color. We found clear evidence for feature-based suppression, and this effect was similar for the two age groups. These findings indicate that feature-based suppression develops early and may already be established by ages 5–6. More broadly, they are consistent with accounts in which suppression emerges through implicit learning or habituation-like mechanisms that are operational early in development. item.title: Beliefs about the causal interdependence of virtues and vices.
item.content:encoded: How do people think different positive and negative moral traits (i.e., virtues and vices) affect one another? For example, do they think that improving one virtue (e.g., honesty) will facilitate improvements in another virtue (e.g., compassion)? Do people believe in “master virtues” that, when improved, have disproportionate positive impacts on other moral virtues? Here, we examine perceived causal interdependence among 15 moral virtues and 13 moral vices. Across four studies, participants indicated their beliefs about how increasing their virtues would impact their other virtues (Study 1; 275 Prolific participants), how increasing their vices would impact their other vices (Study 2; 423 undergraduate students), and how increases in virtues would affect vices (or vice versa; Studies 3 and 4; 337 undergraduate students and 298 Prolific participants). We find people generally believe in facilitation effects, where improving one trait improves other traits and worsening one trait worsens other traits. Specifically, people believe that increasing one virtue tends to increase other virtues (Study 1) and decrease other vices (Studies 3 and 4). Similarly, people believe that increasing one vice tends to increase other vices (Study 2) and decrease other virtues (Studies 3 and 4). Perceived trade-offs were rare and involved laziness and cowardice decreasing or being decreased by other vices. There was little evidence for beliefs in a “master virtue.” However, we find some evidence that people think cruelty and greed are disproportionately impactful “master vices.” These results enhance our understanding of lay moral concepts by painting a comprehensive picture of people’s beliefs about the causal interdependence among moral virtues and vices. item.title: Enacted love: Capitalization responses signal love, including toward strangers.
item.content:encoded: What behavior is seen as “love” and why does it matter? We theorize active-constructive responding to another’s disclosure of good news is prototypical “enacted love” and test hypotheses about implications for a loving person’s relationship development. We use three distinct methods—dyadic interactions between romantic couples (Study 1, N = 160), real spontaneous responses to a stranger’s good news (Study 2, N = 204), and observation of others’ real capitalization responses to a stranger’s good news (Studies 3–5, N = 97, 105, and 402, respectively)—to assess convergent and discriminant evidence for the construct. Study 2 uses experience sampling to track the development of capitalization respondents’ social lives over time. Studies 4 and 5 use within-subjects experiments to test hypotheses that loving behavior could influence others’ interactions with loving people. Results have theoretical implications for close relationships and the concept of “loving one’s neighbor,” plus practical implications for building bridges in a divided society. item.title: Investigating how reward retroactively improves memory for associations and items: A registered report.
item.content:encoded: Given we cannot remember all our experiences, it seems intuitive that we should prioritize events of consequence, like those that lead to a reward. However, rewards have had inconsistent effects on people’s memory for preceding neutral experiences in experiments, raising questions as to whether our minds are equipped to remember adaptively. Here, we used online testing in a registered report to investigate whether rewards tend to retroactively enhance certain types of memories. Consistent with prior research and theories involving how dopamine modulates the hippocampus, we hypothesized that reward would retroactively enhance memory in a delay-dependent manner, emerging only after a period of consolidation. Crucially, we further predicted that this long-delay modulation of memory would be stronger for associative memory than for item recognition—a factor not previously considered despite its clear theoretical grounding. Our planned confirmatory analyses did not reveal any evidence for retroactive effects of reward on either associative or item memory. However, in exploratory analyses examining only individuals who were behaviorally sensitive to the reward manipulation, as measured by an independent task, we found evidence that reward retroactively enhanced associative—but not item—memory in a delay-dependent manner. This work sheds light on important open questions about the mechanisms by which reward retroactively enhances memory, elucidating the conditions under which this key aspect of adaptive memory emerges. item.title: What can machine learning discover about the nature of emotion?
item.author: Kieran McVeigh, Andrew Smart, Ajay B. Satpute, Karen S. Quigley, Jordan E. Theriault-Brown, Lisa Feldman Barrett
item.content:encoded: The science of emotion increasingly relies on machine learning (ML) in the hope of making objective discoveries that resolve century-long debates. We examine research strategies in two main research traditions and show how confirmation bias can arise when theory-based hypotheses are evaluated using theory-laden sampling strategies, model specifications, and inferences. Each tradition manifests its theoretical differences in its ML methods, and, therefore, ML methods cannot settle those differences. The reciprocal relationships between starting assumptions, findings, and conclusions illustrate that ML investigations of emotion, like all scientific investigations, are never free from human experience and beliefs; however, they can be made less biased through a theory-aware research strategy to generate more justified knowledge about emotion.

item.title: Mate preferences and the compatibility puzzle
item.author: Paul W. Eastwick, Amy A.Z. Zhao, Brendan P. Zietsch
item.content:encoded: Researchers and laypeople commonly assume that romantic attraction depends, at least in part, on whether potential partners possess the traits that a person says they want. Yet recent studies suggest that such preference-matching effects (Preference × Trait statistical interactions) are often surprisingly small or even absent. Possible psychological explanations include (i) mate choice is multivariate, and so the matching effect for any given trait is heavily constrained, and (ii) traits permit flexible interpretations, in that the same trait can be interpreted differently depending on the partner to whom the trait belongs. Compatibility may derive not mainly from the matching of preferences and traits but rather from the way that two people recurrently extend and build upon shared positive experiences over time.

item.title: Organization of neuropeptide signaling: cross-species insights from small model organisms
item.author: Meet Zandawala, Alessandro Filosa, Isabel Beets
item.content:encoded: Neuropeptides are ancient signaling molecules that modulate neural circuit function and behavior across the animal kingdom. Model organisms such as Caenorhabditis elegans, Drosophila melanogaster, and zebrafish serve as powerful in vivo models for deciphering the organization of neuropeptidergic signaling, owing to their smaller nervous systems, genetic tractability, and the growing availability of neural connectomes. In this article, we review how these organisms have advanced current understanding of neuropeptidergic transmission across three interconnected themes: (i) the roles of peptides in sensory–motor transformations, (ii) the conservation and divergence of peptidergic expression and network architecture across species, and (iii) the diversity of neurotransmission strategies employed by single neurons. Finally, we highlight recent technological innovations as well as open questions that could shape this field in the coming years.
